title: Thai grammar
variety: Central Thai (standard Thai, as spoken in Bangkok)
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Thai, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Central Thai, in Thai script with a reading in Latin letters that shows the tones.

units.title: Thoughts, stories and what people said

lessons.title: Say hello, thank you and sorry politely
lessons.summary: Greet people, thank them and say sorry, with the little word that makes Thai polite: {{ครับ|kráp}} if you're a man, {{ค่ะ|kâ}} if you're a woman.
lessons.topic: The polite end words {{ครับ|kráp}}, {{ค่ะ|kâ}} and {{คะ|ká}}; {{สวัสดี|sà-wàt-dii}}, {{ขอบคุณ|kɔ̀ɔp-kun}}, {{ขอโทษ|kɔ̌ɔ-tôot}}, {{ไม่เป็นไร|mâi bpen rai}}

goal.t: สวัสดีครับ ยินดีที่ได้รู้จักครับ
goal.r: sà-wàt-dii kráp, yin-dii tîi dâai rúu-jàk kráp

dialog.t: สวัสดีค่ะ
สวัสดีครับ
ยินดีที่ได้รู้จักค่ะ
ยินดีเช่นกันครับ

blocks.p: Listen to the end of each line. Nit always finishes with {{ค่ะ|kâ}}, Tom with {{ครับ|kráp}}. These little words have no meaning of their own: they make what you say polite and friendly, and Thais add them to almost every sentence when they talk to someone they don't know well.

blocks.means: a small word that changes how a sentence sounds (polite, friendly, a question) rather than what it says. Thai puts them at the end of the sentence: {{ครับ|kráp}}, {{ค่ะ|kâ}}.

blocks.p: **The speaker decides.** Which one you use depends on **who is speaking**, not on who you're talking to. A man says {{ครับ|kráp}}, to everyone. A woman says {{ค่ะ|kâ}}, and in a question she changes it to {{คะ|ká}}.

table: in a statement or an answer
on its own: “yes, OK, I'm listening”

blocks.p: **Tones.** In Thai the pitch of your voice is part of the word: {{ค่ะ|kâ}} and {{คะ|ká}} are different words only because of their tone. The reading shows the tone with a mark over the vowel: **a** (no mark) mid, level; **à** low; **â** falling, like a firm “No.”; **á** high; **ǎ** rising, like a surprised “Huh?”.

ex.t: ขอบคุณครับ
ขอบคุณมากค่ะ
ขอโทษครับ

blocks.tip: {{สวัสดี|sà-wàt-dii}} is “hello” and also “goodbye”. Thais say it with a {{ไหว้|wâai}}: palms pressed together in front of the chest and a small bow of the head.

lessons.title: Say your name and where you're from
lessons.summary: Say who you are and where you come from, and ask someone the same: your first Thai conversation.
lessons.topic: {{ผม|pǒm}} / {{ฉัน|chǎn}} “I”, {{คุณ|kun}} “you”; {{ชื่อ|chʉ̂ʉ}} and {{มาจาก|maa jàak}} with no “is”; the question word at the end

goal.t: ผมชื่อทอมครับ ผมมาจากอเมริกาครับ
goal.r: pǒm chʉ̂ʉ tɔm kráp, pǒm maa jàak à-mee-rí-gaa kráp
goal.tr: My name is Tom. I'm from America.

dialog.t: สวัสดีค่ะ ฉันชื่อนิดค่ะ
dialog.r: sà-wàt-dii kâ, chǎn chʉ̂ʉ nít kâ

dialog.tr: I'm from America. And you, Nit?

dialog.t: ฉันมาจากเชียงใหม่ค่ะ

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **“I” for a man, “I” for a woman.** A man says {{ผม|pǒm}}, a woman says {{ฉัน|chǎn}} (in formal speech, {{ดิฉัน|dì-chǎn}}). It goes with the end word: {{ผม…ครับ|pǒm … kráp}}, {{ฉัน…ค่ะ|chǎn … kâ}}.

**“You”.** The polite “you” is {{คุณ|kun}}. It also goes before a name, like “Mr” or “Ms”: {{คุณนิด|kun nít}}. Thais often say the person's name where English says “you”: {{คุณทอมมาจากไหนคะ|kun tɔm maa jàak nǎi ká}} is, word for word, “Mr Tom comes from where?”.

**No “is”.** {{ชื่อ|chʉ̂ʉ}} means “to be called”, so {{ผมชื่อทอม|pǒm chʉ̂ʉ tɔm}} (“I am-called Tom”) needs nothing else. {{มาจาก|maa jàak}} is “come from”: {{ผมมาจากอเมริกา|pǒm maa jàak à-mee-rí-gaa}} “I come from America”.

blocks.means: a word that asks for a piece of information: what, where, who, when.

blocks.p: **Asking.** The question word goes where the answer will go, at the end: {{คุณชื่ออะไร|kun chʉ̂ʉ à-rai}} “you are-called what?”, {{มาจากไหน|maa jàak nǎi}} “come from where?”. To answer, put your answer in its place.

table: {{คุณชื่ออะไร|kun chʉ̂ʉ à-rai}} What's your name?
{{ผมชื่อทอม|pǒm chʉ̂ʉ tɔm}} My name is Tom.
{{คุณมาจากไหน|kun maa jàak nǎi}} Where are you from?
{{ฉันมาจากเชียงใหม่|chǎn maa jàak chiiang-mài}} I'm from Chiang Mai.

blocks.p: **Leaving out “I”.** Once it's clear who you're talking about, Thai drops the pronoun: {{ชื่อทอมครับ|chʉ̂ʉ tɔm kráp}} “(I'm) Tom.” This is normal and polite. And {{แล้ว…ล่ะ|lɛ́ɛo … lâ}} turns the question round: {{แล้วคุณล่ะ|lɛ́ɛo kun lâ}} “and you?”.

ex.t: ฉันชื่อแอนนาค่ะ
คุณชื่ออะไรครับ
มาจากอังกฤษค่ะ
คุณมาจากไหนคะ
ผมมาจากแคนาดาครับ

blocks.tip: **Reading the vowels.** A doubled letter is a long vowel ({{มา|maa}}, a long “ah”). **ɛ** is the e of “bed”, **ɔ** the aw of “law”, **ʉ** an “oo” said with the lips spread, **ə** the u of “fur”. **bp** and **dt** are a p and a t with no puff of air (as in “spin”, “stop”); plain **p**, **t** and **k** have the puff, as in “pin”.

lessons.title: Say what you do and what you are
lessons.summary: Say your job and your nationality, ask someone what they do, and say what you're not.
lessons.topic: {{เป็น|bpen}} “to be” + a noun; {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} and {{ไม่ได้เป็น|mâi dâai bpen}} “not”; {{คน|kon}} + a country

goal.r: chǎn bpen kruu sɔ̌ɔn paa-sǎa ang-grìt kâ

dialog.t: คุณทำงานอะไรครับ
ฉันเป็นครูสอนภาษาอังกฤษค่ะ แล้วคุณล่ะคะ
dialog.r: chǎn bpen kruu sɔ̌ɔn paa-sǎa ang-grìt kâ, lɛ́ɛo kun lâ ká
dialog.tr: I'm an English teacher. And you?

dialog.t: ผมเป็นหมอครับ คุณเป็นคนอเมริกันใช่ไหมครับ
dialog.r: pǒm bpen mɔ̌ɔ kráp, kun bpen kon à-mee-rí-gan châi mǎi kráp
dialog.tr: I'm a doctor. You're American, right?

dialog.t: ไม่ใช่ค่ะ ฉันเป็นคนอังกฤษค่ะ
dialog.r: mâi châi kâ, chǎn bpen kon ang-grìt kâ

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: teacher, coffee, Bangkok.
a word for an action or a state: go, eat, teach, be.

blocks.p: **เป็น, “to be”.** To say what someone *is* (a job, a nationality, a role), put the verb {{เป็น|bpen}} between the person and the noun: {{ผมเป็นหมอ|pǒm bpen mɔ̌ɔ}} “I am doctor”. Thai has no word for “a”: the noun alone is enough.

**Nationalities.** “A Thai” is {{คนไทย|kon tai}}, literally “person Thai”: {{คน|kon}} “person”, then the country. {{คนอังกฤษ|kon ang-grìt}} “English”, {{คนญี่ปุ่น|kon yîi-bpùn}} “Japanese”, {{คนอเมริกัน|kon à-mee-rí-gan}} “American”. A language is {{ภาษา|paa-sǎa}} “language” + the country: {{ภาษาไทย|paa-sǎa tai}}, {{ภาษาอังกฤษ|paa-sǎa ang-grìt}}.

**Not.** To say what someone is *not*, use {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} in place of {{เป็น|bpen}}: {{ผมไม่ใช่หมอ|pǒm mâi-châi mɔ̌ɔ}} “I'm not a doctor”. {{ไม่ได้เป็น|mâi dâai bpen}} means the same: {{ผมไม่ได้เป็นหมอ|pǒm mâi dâai bpen mɔ̌ɔ}}. On its own, {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} is “no, that's not right”.

**Asking someone's job.** {{คุณทำงานอะไร|kun tam-ngaan à-rai}} “you work what?”: {{ทำงาน|tam-ngaan}} is “to work”. You can answer with {{เป็น|bpen}} and a job, or say where you work: {{ผมทำงานที่ธนาคาร|pǒm tam-ngaan tîi tá-naa-kaan}} “I work at a bank”.

แม่ฉันเป็นพยาบาลค่ะ

ex.t: ผมทำงานที่ธนาคารครับ
คุณทำงานอะไรคะ

blocks.tip: {{เป็น|bpen}} is only for nouns: a teacher, a Thai, a friend. To say what something is *like* (good, hot, tired), Thai uses no “be” at all: that's the next lesson.

lessons.title: Say what something is like
lessons.summary: Say the food is delicious, the room is big or you're tired: in Thai, describing words need no “is”.
lessons.topic: Adjectives work as verbs (no {{เป็น|bpen}}); the adjective after the noun; {{มาก|mâak}} “very”, {{ไม่|mâi}} “not”

goal.t: อาหารไทยอร่อยมากค่ะ

dialog.t: อร่อยไหมครับ
อร่อยมากค่ะ
แต่เผ็ดนิดหน่อยครับ
ร้านนี้สวยด้วยค่ะ
dialog.tr: And this place is pretty, too.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, hot, delicious, tired.

blocks.p: **No “is” with describing words.** In Thai a word like “delicious”, “big” or “tired” works like a verb all by itself: {{อร่อย|à-rɔ̀i}} means “to be delicious”. So {{อาหารอร่อย|aa-hǎan à-rɔ̀i}} is a whole sentence: “the food is delicious”. Never put {{เป็น|bpen}} before an adjective.

**After the noun.** The describing word comes after the thing it describes: {{อาหารไทย|aa-hǎan tai}} “food Thai” = Thai food, {{ห้องใหญ่|hɔ̂ng yài}} “room big” = a big room. The same words can also be a sentence, “the room is big”: the situation tells you which.
**Very, a little, not.** {{มาก|mâak}} “very, a lot” and {{นิดหน่อย|nít-nɔ̀i}} “a little” go after the adjective. {{ไม่|mâi}} “not” goes before it.

table: {{ร้อนมาก|rɔ́ɔn mâak}} very hot
{{ไม่ร้อน|mâi rɔ́ɔn}} not hot
{{แพงมาก|pɛɛng mâak}} very expensive
{{ไม่แพง|mâi pɛɛng}} not expensive
{{เผ็ดมาก|pèt mâak}} very spicy
{{ไม่เผ็ด|mâi pèt}} not spicy

ex.t: วันนี้ร้อนมากค่ะ
ห้องนี้ใหญ่ครับ
ผมเหนื่อยครับ
ฉันหิวมากค่ะ
กาแฟไม่หวานค่ะ
ภาษาไทยไม่ยากครับ

blocks.tip: Feelings work the same way: {{หิว|hǐu}} “hungry”, {{เหนื่อย|nʉ̀ai}} “tired”, {{สบาย|sà-baai}} “well, comfortable”. {{สบายดี|sà-baai-dii}} from the first lesson is “well and good”: I'm fine.

mistakes.wrong: อาหารเป็นอร่อย
mistakes.right: อาหารอร่อย
mistakes.why: A describing word needs no “is”: {{เป็น|bpen}} is only for nouns (a teacher, a Thai).
The describing word comes **after** the thing.
{{มาก|mâak}} “very” goes after the word it makes stronger.

practice.q: Which one means “I'm tired”?
options: {{ผมเป็นเหนื่อย|pǒm bpen nʉ̀ai}}
practice.why: No {{เป็น|bpen}} before a describing word.

practice.q: Choose: {{ไม่|mâi}} “not” or {{มาก|mâak}} “very”.
practice.t: กาแฟ___หวานค่ะ
practice.why: “Not” comes before the word: {{ไม่หวาน|mâi wǎan}}.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Which sentence needs {{เป็น|bpen}} in Thai?
practice.why: A noun (a teacher) needs {{เป็น|bpen}}: {{ฉันเป็นครู|chǎn bpen kruu}}. Describing words don't: {{ฉันหิว|chǎn hǐu}}, {{ร้อน|rɔ́ɔn}}.

lessons.title: Ask yes/no questions and answer them
lessons.summary: Ask “Do you like…?” or “Is it…?” with one little word at the end, and answer the Thai way: with the verb.
lessons.topic: {{ไหม|mǎi}} at the end of a question; answering with the verb or the adjective; {{ใช่ไหม|châi mǎi}} “…, right?”

goal.t: คุณชอบอาหารไทยไหมคะ
goal.r: kun chɔ̂ɔp aa-hǎan tai mǎi ká

dialog.t: คุณชอบอาหารไทยไหมคะ
dialog.r: kun chɔ̂ɔp aa-hǎan tai mǎi ká

dialog.t: ชอบครับ ชอบมากครับ
ต้มยำเผ็ดไหมคะ
เผ็ดนิดหน่อยครับ แต่อร่อย
คุณมาจากอเมริกาใช่ไหมคะ
dialog.r: kun maa jàak à-mee-rí-gaa châi mǎi ká

dialog.t: ใช่ครับ

blocks.p: **Asking.** Take any statement and put {{ไหม|mǎi}} at the end: it becomes a yes/no question. Nothing else changes: no new word order, no “do”. {{คุณชอบกาแฟ|kun chɔ̂ɔp gaa-fɛɛ}} “you like coffee” → {{คุณชอบกาแฟไหม|kun chɔ̂ɔp gaa-fɛɛ mǎi}} “do you like coffee?”. The end word comes last: {{…ไหมครับ|… mǎi kráp}}, {{…ไหมคะ|… mǎi ká}}.

**Answering.** Thai has no all-purpose “yes”. You answer with the verb or the adjective of the question: {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}} “(I) like (it)”, or {{ไม่ชอบ|mâi chɔ̂ɔp}} “(I) don't like (it)”. Then your end word.

table: {{หิวไหม|hǐu mǎi}} Are you hungry?
{{ชอบไหม|chɔ̂ɔp mǎi}} Do you like it?
{{เผ็ดไหม|pèt mǎi}} Is it spicy?

blocks.p: **…, right?** To check something you think is true, end with {{ใช่ไหม|châi mǎi}}: {{คุณเป็นคนไทยใช่ไหม|kun bpen kon tai châi mǎi}} “you're Thai, right?”. Now the answer is {{ใช่|châi}} “yes, that's right” or {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} “no”.

ไม่หิวค่ะ
คุณเหนื่อยไหมคะ

blocks.tip: **Listen to the tones.** {{ไหม|mǎi}} (rising) asks; {{ไม่|mâi}} (falling) means “not”. In everyday speech {{ไหม|mǎi}} is usually said with a high tone, mái, and in messages you'll often see it written {{มั้ย|mái}}.

mistakes.why: The question word is {{ไหม|mǎi}}, rising. {{ไม่|mâi}}, falling, means “not”.

mistakes.why: {{ใช่|châi}} means “that's right”: it answers a {{ใช่ไหม|châi mǎi}} question. To “do you like…?”, answer with the verb, {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}}.

lessons.title: Point and ask what things are
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, name things, and ask what something is called in Thai.
lessons.topic: {{นี่|nîi}}, {{นั่น|nân}}, {{โน่น|nôon}}; {{คือ|kʉʉ}} “is”; {{เรียกว่า|rîiak wâa}} “is called”

goal.t: นี่คืออะไรคะ

dialog.t: นี่คืออะไรครับ
ทุเรียนค่ะ
แล้วนั่นล่ะครับ
นั่นมังคุดค่ะ อร่อยมากนะคะ
dialog.r: nân mang-kút kâ, à-rɔ̀i mâak ná ká

dialog.t: โน่นเรียกว่าอะไรครับ
dialog.tr: And what's that over there called?

dialog.t: เงาะค่ะ

blocks.p: **This, that, that over there.** On their own, pointing: {{นี่|nîi}} “this (here, near me)”, {{นั่น|nân}} “that (near you)”, {{โน่น|nôon}} “that (over there, far from us both)”. All three have a falling tone.

**คือ, “is”.** {{นี่คืออะไร|nîi kʉʉ à-rai}} is “this is what?”, and the answer puts the name in place of {{อะไร|à-rai}}: {{นี่คือทุเรียน|nîi kʉʉ tú-riian}} “this is durian”. In quick speech {{คือ|kʉʉ}} is often left out: {{นั่นอะไร|nân à-rai}}, {{นั่นมังคุด|nân mang-kút}}. Or just say the name: {{ทุเรียนค่ะ|tú-riian kâ}}.

**เป็น or คือ?** Both come before a noun. {{เป็น|bpen}} says what group or job someone belongs to: {{ฉันเป็นครู|chǎn bpen kruu}} “I'm a teacher (one of many)”. {{คือ|kʉʉ}} says *which one* something is, or what it means: {{นี่คือบ้านของฉัน|nîi kʉʉ bâan kɔ̌ɔng chǎn}} “this is my house”.
**What's it called?** {{เรียกว่า|rîiak wâa}} means “is called”: {{ภาษาไทยเรียกว่าอะไร|paa-sǎa tai rîiak wâa à-rai}} “in Thai, (it's) called what?”. The answer: {{เรียกว่า…|rîiak wâa …}} and the word.

blocks.tip: Later you'll meet {{นี้|níi}} and {{นั้น|nán}}, with a high tone, which go *after* a noun: “this shirt”, “that man”. {{นี่|nîi}} and {{นั่น|nân}}, falling, stand on their own.

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.summary: Introduce people and talk about them: he, she, we, they, and the Thai way of calling people by name or by a family word.
lessons.topic: {{เขา|kǎo}} “he, she”, {{เรา|rao}} “we”, {{พวกเขา|pûuak-kǎo}} “they”, {{มัน|man}} “it”; names and {{พี่|pîi}} / {{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}} in place of “you”

goal.t: นี่คือคุณสมชายค่ะ เขาเป็นหมอค่ะ
goal.r: nîi kʉʉ kun sǒm-chaai kâ, kǎo bpen mɔ̌ɔ kâ
goal.tr: This is Somchai. He's a doctor.

dialog.t: นี่คือคุณสมชายค่ะ เขาเป็นเพื่อนฉันค่ะ
dialog.r: nîi kʉʉ kun sǒm-chaai kâ, kǎo bpen pʉ̂ʉan chǎn kâ
dialog.tr: This is Somchai. He's my friend.

dialog.t: สวัสดีครับ ยินดีที่ได้รู้จักครับ
dialog.r: sà-wàt-dii kráp, yin-dii tîi dâai rúu-jàk kráp

dialog.t: แล้วเขาเป็นใครครับ
เขาชื่อฝนค่ะ เขาเป็นครู เราทำงานด้วยกันค่ะ
dialog.r: kǎo chʉ̂ʉ fǒn kâ, kǎo bpen kruu, rao tam-ngaan dûai-gan kâ
dialog.tr: Her name is Fon. She's a teacher. We work together.

blocks.p: **He and she are one word.** {{เขา|kǎo}} means “he” *and* “she” (and “him”, “her”). Anna uses it for Somchai and for Fon: who is meant is clear from the situation.

**We, they, it.** {{เรา|rao}} is “we, us”. For “they”, add {{พวก|pûuak}} “group”: {{พวกเขา|pûuak-kǎo}} (or just {{เขา|kǎo}} again). {{มัน|man}} is “it”, for animals and things; but for things Thai usually says nothing at all: {{อร่อยมาก|à-rɔ̀i mâak}} “(it's) delicious”.

table: animals and things; often left out

blocks.p: **Names and family words.** Thais often use a name where English says “you” or “he”: {{คุณนิดไปไหนคะ|kun nít bpai nǎi ká}} “where is Nit going?”, asked to Nit herself. With friends and people about your age, Thais use family words: {{พี่|pîi}} “older brother or sister” for someone a little older, {{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}} “younger brother or sister” for someone younger. Even with a waiter or a shop assistant: {{พี่ครับ|pîi kráp}} “excuse me!” (to someone a bit older).

ex.t: เขาเป็นคนไทยครับ
เขาชื่ออะไรคะ
ex.tr: What's his name? / What's her name?

ex.t: เราเป็นนักเรียนค่ะ
พวกเขามาจากญี่ปุ่นครับ
มันน่ารักมากค่ะ
พี่ครับ ขอเมนูหน่อยครับ
ex.r: pîi kráp, kɔ̌ɔ mee-nuu nɔ̀i kráp
ex.tr: Excuse me, could I have the menu?
ex.note: to a waiter a little older than you

blocks.tip: Calling someone {{พี่|pîi}} or {{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}} is warm, not rude: it treats them like family. {{คุณ|kun}} is safe with anyone, though between friends it can sound a little distant.

mistakes.right: เขาเป็นครู
mistakes.why: {{มัน|man}} is for animals and things; used for a person it's rude. For people, {{เขา|kǎo}}.
